passage:
Wednesday night
Called home three times today. Once to ask Papa whether to take the morning or evening section of statistics. Once to ask Ma if the blue shirt was okay for the interview. Once just to hear them say "well done" about my quiz marks.
Kishore laughed at me in the mess: "You're twenty, not ten." It stung.
The real thing I didn't say on any call: I want to apply for the six-month exchange in Pune. Theatre and design. Ma cried last year when I only moved to the hostel. Papa says family should stay close.
I filled in the application and didn't submit it. Every time I imagine telling them, I feel like I'm betraying them. I also feel like I'm betraying me.
Ujjwal

qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: Why does Ujjwal feel like betraying both the family and self?
qa.a: Ujjwal loves the parents and wants their praise, but also wants the exchange, so choosing either way feels like letting someone down.

qa.a: Ujjwal could first tell Papa and Ma what is exciting about theatre and design, before submitting, so the wish is spoken rather than hidden.

qa.a: They may feel close and needed, perhaps without realising Ujjwal is seeking permission for every choice while hiding a bigger wish.

grounding: In a diary, a young adult from a close family seeks parents' approval for everything and feels guilty about a wish of their own.

Appa will go quiet. And then I'll feel I've hurt them for something selfish." Farida was silent a moment. "Is it selfish to want your own thing?" Deepika watched the water. "I don't know. In the student hostel in Nairobi, Wanjiru held up two dresses for the class photo and then video-called her mother to choose. Vera, her roommate, watched from the top bunk.
It wasn't just dresses. Wanjiru's mother had helped pick her courses, her part-time job, even which study group to join. After every good thing Wanjiru did, she called home to hear, 'Well done, my girl.'
Tonight's call was about something bigger. A photography club was offering a free weekend workshop in Naivasha, and Wanjiru wanted it badly. But the family fundraiser for her cousin's school fees was the same Saturday.
'Mum says it's my choice,' she told Vera afterwards. 'But I heard her voice go quiet.' She sat on the bed with the workshop form in her lap and rubbed her eyes. 'Why do I feel like a bad daughter for wanting one weekend?'

qa.q: Where was the photography workshop being held?
qa.a: In Naivasha.

qa.q: Why does Wanjiru feel like 'a bad daughter' for wanting the workshop?
qa.a: She loves her family and depends on her mother's praise; wanting something different from the family plan feels like letting them down, so the wish arrives with guilt.

qa.a: She could decide about the workshop herself before calling home, then share her reasons with her mother; one small decision of her own can hold love and duty together.

In the placement office at the college in Thrissur, Usha stared at two offer letters: one from a firm in Kochi, forty minutes from home, and one from the design studio in Bengaluru she had dreamed about since first year.
'Which one do you want?' asked Imran sir, the placement officer.
'I'll ask Appa,' Usha said at once, already dialling. It was what she always did: which elective, which project, even which font for her resume. Appa's 'good choice, molu' made everything feel right.
This time Appa said, 'Kochi is close. Amma will be happy.' Usha said, 'Yes, Appa,' and put the phone down.
Her eyes filled anyway. 'I do love them,' she told Imran sir. 'I just wanted Bengaluru.'
Imran sir pushed the tissue box across. 'Both can be true. Take a day. Decide for yourself, then tell them why.'

qa.q: Where was the design studio that offered Usha a job?
qa.a: In Bengaluru.

qa.q: Why did Usha's eyes fill after she said 'Yes, Appa'?
qa.a: She loves her parents and wants Appa's approval, yet her own wish was Bengaluru; agreeing felt dutiful but meant giving up what she wanted, so guilt and sadness mixed.

qa.q: What did Imran sir advise, and why is it a good step?
qa.a: To take a day, decide for herself and then tell her parents why; it lets Usha's own wish count while keeping her family close.

qa.q: How might Appa see the call about the two offers?
qa.a: Appa probably thinks he simply gave helpful advice, since Usha always asks him, and may not know she was hoping for a different answer.

grounding: A young woman who asks her father about every decision agrees to the job he prefers, then feels the pull of her own wish.

passage: Every decision Jasleen made, she ran past her father first. Which elective, which kurta for the college fest, whether to cut her hair. Bhupen always had an answer, and his 'shabaash, puttar' felt like sunshine. So when the design firm in Bengaluru offered her a six-month internship, she didn't tell anyone for three days. She sat on the terrace of their house in Ludhiana with the email open on her phone, feeling sick. She wanted it more than anything. And she knew Papa's face would fall; he had always said she'd work in the family printing business after college. On the fourth day she brought him tea and said, 'Papa, I got an offer.' He read it slowly. He didn't say shabaash. He said, 'Bengaluru is very far.' That night Jasleen lay awake, torn between the offer and the guilt of wanting it.

qa.q: Where was the design firm that offered the internship?
qa.a: It was in Bengaluru.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen feel sick sitting on the terrace?
qa.a: She wanted the internship badly, but loved her father and felt guilty that her wish went against his plans, so love and duty pulled against each other.

qa.q: What could Jasleen do to honour both love and her own wish?
qa.a: She could talk openly with Papa about why the internship matters, ask about his worries, and look for a plan that respects both, such as returning after six months.

qa.q: How might Bhupen feel reading the email?
qa.a: Bhupen probably felt worried and a little sad, imagining his daughter far away and his hopes for the family business changing.

passage: Until last year I had never made a decision without asking Amma first. Not which shoes, not which friends, not which college. Her smile was the thing I worked for. So when I realised I wanted to switch from chartered accountancy to journalism, I couldn't sleep for a week. Amma had framed my CA foundation certificate. She'd told every relative. Every time I imagined telling her, I felt a thick guilt in my throat, as if wanting something for myself were a kind of stealing. When I finally told her over Sunday lunch, she went very quiet. Then she said, 'Ujjwal, I wanted you safe. I didn't know you were unhappy.' She didn't say yes that day. But she didn't say no either. Now I'm in my first semester of journalism, and she still calls every evening. Some days I still check her face before I choose anything. I'm learning not to.

qa.q: What had Amma framed?
qa.a: She had framed Ujjwal's CA foundation certificate.

qa.q: Why did wanting journalism feel 'like stealing' to Ujjwal?
qa.a: Ujjwal loved Amma and depended on her approval, so wanting something different brought a thick sense of guilt, as if taking something from her.

qa.q: What helped Ujjwal move forward?
qa.a: Telling Amma honestly over lunch, which let her explain that she wanted Ujjwal safe and hadn't known about the unhappiness.

qa.q: How did Amma respond to the news?
qa.a: She went quiet, explained she had wanted Ujjwal safe and hadn't known about the unhappiness, and neither agreed nor refused that day.

Hostel warden's note, girls' hostel, 3rd year.
Nirmala is a kind, reliable student. I have noticed that she calls her mother before nearly every decision, even small ones: which elective, which kurta for the college fest, whether to join the NSS camp.
This week she was offered a summer research internship in Bengaluru. She was glowing when she told her roommate Sabina. Then she called home. Her parents want her in Madurai for the summer, as usual.
Afterward she sat in the common room a long time. Sabina told me she kept saying, “I'm a bad daughter for even wanting it.”
She loves her parents deeply; her own wishes are still finding room beside that love.
What I did next: I sat with her and told her that wanting something different is not the same as not loving her family. I have booked her a college counsellor appointment for Thursday, before she replies to the offer.

qa.q: Where was Nirmala offered a research internship?
qa.a: She was offered it in Bengaluru for the summer.

qa.q: Why did Nirmala keep saying she was a bad daughter?
qa.a: She felt guilty for having a wish that differed from her parents', torn between love for them and wanting the internship.

qa.q: What did the warden do that could help Nirmala?
qa.a: Reassured her that wanting something different isn't a lack of love, and booked a counsellor appointment so she can think it through.

qa.q: How might Sabina feel watching her roommate?
qa.a: Sabina probably feels worried and sympathetic, having seen Nirmala go from glowing to sad.

passage:
Monday night.
I got the job offer from the Delhi publishing house. My first real one. I screamed into my pillow.
Then I did what I always do. I called Ma before I even told Bhavna. And Ma went quiet, then said, “Delhi is so far, beta. What about the job in Lucknow, near us?”
The Lucknow job is fine. But it isn't books.
Bhavna came in and saw my face. She said, “You want Delhi.” I said I didn't know. That's a lie. I do know. I just can't want it without feeling like I'm abandoning them.
I've asked Ma about everything, my stream, my college, my haircut. Her “good choice” has been my compass. Now it points one way and I point the other.
I love them. I also love this. I'm going to call Ma tomorrow and just tell her how much.
— Ganga

Is the blue kurta fine for the college function? Papa always had an answer, and when he said, "Shabaash, beta," she slept well.

"Yes, Papa. You're right."
She ended the call and sat on the parapet, holding the old camera her Nani had given her. She felt guilty for wanting it at all, and guilty for how badly she still wanted it.

The dorm in Vancouver was quiet at eleven, which was morning in Seoul, so Jin called home. He told his mother about the lab report, the grocery list, even which bus he took. "Good choice," she said to each, and he smiled at the screen.
Then he mentioned the summer. The design studio downtown had offered him an internship. It was the thing he had been sketching toward all year.
His mother paused. "Your father thought you would come home and help at the restaurant. Your aunt is getting older."
"I know. I was only saying they offered."
After the call, his roommate Marek found him staring at the offer email. "You look like you lost."
"I feel like a bad son for even wanting it," Jin said. "And I still want it."

Dear Irfan,
Writing from home. Navratri lights everywhere, and Mummy has asked me three times whether I'm eating properly.
I need to tell someone this. Before I buy anything, even a shirt, I send Papa a photo and wait for "Very nice, beta." Before I told my professor I'd take the research project, I called home first. When Papa said "Good choice", I felt like I could breathe.

You always seem to know what you want. How do you do it without feeling like you're betraying someone?
Darshan
